1.motto: To the most illustrious Maximilian, Duke of Milan. On the emblem of the Duchy of Milan.

reading: An infant leaping from the jaws of a coiling serpent
is the noble crest of your lineage.
We have seen that the king of Pella [Alexander] bore such coins,
and with them he too glorified his own line,
teaching that he was begotten of Ammon, his mother deceived by the serpent's likeness,
and that he was the offspring of a divine seed.
He comes forth through the mouth; thus, they say, certain serpents give birth —
or is it because Pallas was born this way from the head of Jupiter?
To the Bituriges the ram gives their emblem, to the Hedui the little sow.
To these peoples my homeland owes its origin —
the land the maidens called sacred "Mediolanum":
for so it sounds in the old Gallic tongue.
Where Minerva was once worshipped, now, the godhead changed,
is Thecla, before the house of the Virgin Mother.
Its emblem is the wool-bearing sow, a creature of double form,
bristling sharp on one side, soft-fleeced on the other.
The Elk (Alce) bears the arms of the Alciati family,
and in its hooves carries [Greek: μηδ' ἓν ἀναβαλλόμενος — "deferring nothing"].
It is well known that Alexander answered thus one who asked him
how he had accomplished so many deeds in so short a time.
"By never," he said, "wishing to delay." And this too is shown
by the Elk,
of which one may wonder whether it is the stronger or the swifter.

reading: Behold how the excellent painter has depicted the boy
— the Trojan [Ganymede] — borne through the loftiest stars by Jupiter's bird.
Who would believe that Jupiter was touched by love for a boy?
Say, whence did the old Maeonian [Homer] invent this?
He in whom counsel, mind, and joy in God hold first place —
he, it is believed, is caught up and stands before highest Jupiter.

5.motto: Human wisdom is folly in the eyes of God.

reading: What shall I say? By what name shall I call
this two-formed monster, which is neither man nor dragon?
But without feet, a man; without upper parts, a serpent —
it may be called a serpent-footed man, or a man-headed serpent.
The man farts out a serpent, and the serpent has belched out a man,
and there is neither an end of the man nor a beginning of the beast.
Thus once Cecrops reigned over learned Athens,
thus too mother Earth brought forth the giants.
This is the figure of the crafty; but one devoid of piety,
who cares only for earthly things — that is what it signifies.
A most beautiful harlot sitting on a royal throne
wears a robe distinguished by purple splendor.
And to all she pours drink from a brimming goblet.
But all around a drunken crowd lies sprawled.
Thus they signify Babylon: which with alluring form
and feigned religion ensnares foolish peoples.

7.motto: Not to you, but to religion.

reading: A slow-footed donkey was carrying the image of Isis,
bearing on its bowed back her venerable mysteries.
So whoever meets it reverently worships the Goddess,
and, bending the knee, offers up pious prayers.
But the donkey believes that such honor is being paid
to itself, and swells up, growing quite proud —
until the driver, checking him with the whip, said:
"You are not a god, little donkey, but you carry a god."

8.motto: One must go where the gods call.

reading: At the crossroads there is a mound of stones: above it rises
a truncated image of a god, fashioned only down to the chest.
It is, then, the mound of Mercury. Traveler, hang
garlands for the god who shows you the right path.
We are all at the crossroads, and on this road of life
we go astray, unless God himself shows us the way.
Let Honor stand depicted, veiled in a Tyrian cloak,
and let naked Truth join her right hand to his.
And let chaste Love stand in the middle, whose temples
a rose encircles — fairer than the Cupid of Dione [Venus].
These signs establish fidelity, which the reverence of honor
fosters, Love nourishes, and Truth brings forth.
This cithara, which from its likeness to a skiff is called "halieutica" [the fisher's],
the Latin Muse claims also as her own.
Accept it, Duke: may this gift please you at this time,
when you are preparing to enter new alliances with your allies.
It is hard, save for a skilled man, to stretch so many strings,
and if even one string [fides — "string," but also "faith"] is not well tuned,
or snaps (which easily happens), all the grace of the shell [lyre] is lost,
and that excellent song will turn out unfit.
So the nobles of Italy come together in alliances; while in concord,
there is nothing to fear, so long as love holds firm among you.
But if someone breaks away (as we very often see),
all that harmony dissolves into nothing.
When he is silent, a fool differs not at all from the wise.
His own tongue and voice are the tell-tale sign of his folly.
Let him, then, press his lips and mark silence with his finger,
and turn himself into the Pharian Harpocrates.

12.motto: Counsels are not to be made public.

reading: The monster which, behind a blind threshold, in dark obscurity,
Daedalus shut away in the Gnosian [Cretan] hiding-places [the labyrinth]:
depicted, the Roman phalanx carries it into battle,
and proud standards gleam with the half-man, half-ox [Minotaur].
They warn us that the secret counsels of leaders ought
to remain hidden. A stratagem, once known, harms its own author.

13.motto: One must not yield even to torture.

reading: The Lioness whom you see fashioned on the Cecropian [Athenian] citadel
was the beloved of Hermodius (do you not know this, stranger?).
Thus it pleased them to show the fierce spirit of this manlike woman
in the likeness of a wild beast, or because she bore just such a name.
Because, tortured on the rack, she betrayed no one
by any disclosure, Iphicrates rendered her tongueless.

14.motto: By counsel and courage the Chimaera is overcome — that is, the stronger and the deceivers.

reading: Bellerophon (as a valiant horseman) was able to overcome the Chimaera,
and lay low the monsters of the Lycian soil.
Thus you too, borne on Pegasus's wings, aim for the heavens,
and with the counsel of your mind tame proud monsters.
Because the cock, crowing, gives the signs of approaching dawn,
and calls the servants' hands back to new tasks,
he is fashioned atop sacred towers; and because the bronze bell
recalls the watchful mind to heavenly things,
there too is a lion. But because, as guardian, he sleeps with open eyes,
he is for that reason placed before the doors of temples.

16.motto: Νῆφε καὶ μέμνησ' ἀπιστεῖν. ἄρθρα ταῦτα τῶν φρενῶν ("Be sober, and remember to distrust: these are the joints of the mind"). One must live soberly, and not believe rashly.

reading: Do not believe — Epicharmus says — be not without sobriety,
these shall be the sinews and limbs of the human mind:
Behold the hand with an eye, believing what it sees. Behold
pennyroyal, the herb of ancient sobriety,
by showing which Heraclitus calmed the crowd,
and soothed it, swollen and heavy with sedition.

greek.original: Νῆφε καὶ μέμνησ' ἀπιστεῖν. ἄρθρα ταῦτα τῶν φρενῶν. Sobriè vivendum: & non temerè credendum.
greek.translation: Be sober, and remember to distrust: these are the joints of the mind. One must live soberly, and not believe rashly.

17.motto: Πῆ παρέβην? Τί δ' ἔρεξα? Τί μοι δέον, οὐκ ἐτελέσθη? ("Where have I transgressed? What have I done? What duty of mine has gone unfulfilled?") What have I overstepped? What have I committed? What have I omitted?

reading: The Samian [Pythagoras], most renowned founder of the Italic sect,
himself enclosed his own teaching in a brief verse:
"Where have you overstepped? What are you doing? What do you leave undone that ought to be done?" —
urging each man to render this same reckoning to himself.
This, it is said, he learned from a flock of flying cranes,
which carry a stone seized in their feet,
lest they halt, or ill winds sweep them off course —
by this same rule human life ought to be governed.

greek.original: Πῆ παρέβην? Τί δ' ἔρεξα? Τί μοι δέον, οὐκ ἐτελέσθη? Quid excessi? quid admisi? quid omisi?
greek.translation: Where have I transgressed? What have I done? What duty of mine has gone unfulfilled? What have I overstepped? What have I committed? What have I omitted?

reading: Two-faced Janus, who know well both what is past and what is to come,
and who see the mocking grimaces behind you (as well as before),
why do they fashion you with so many eyes, so many faces? Is it because
this form teaches that a man ought to be circumspect?
The owl furnishes the emblem of Cecropian Athens,
the owl, among birds the bird of sound counsel.
Deservedly it is consecrated to the service of warlike Minerva,
in the place which the chattering crow had earlier yielded.
All bid us hasten swiftly, and yet also to delay,
lest [the deed] be too headlong, nor the delay too long.
Let this be shown to you by the dart joined with the echeneis [remora fish]:
the fish is slow, while the arrows, once loosed by hand, fly swiftly.
For a long time now, wherever you flee, I pursue you: but now
you are here at last, caught in our snares.
No longer will you be able to escape our strength:
we have gripped the eel tight in a fig leaf.
This is the true likeness of unwed Pallas: hers
is this Dragon, which stands before its mistress's feet.
Why is this creature the goddess's companion? The guarding of all things
is given to it: thus it keeps groves and sacred temples.
Unwed girls must be kept safe
with watchful care: everywhere Love spreads its snares.
Father Bacchus and Pallas, both together,
hold this temple: each the true offspring of Jupiter.
She sprang from his head, he burst from his thigh: to her is owed
the use of the olive, but he first discovered wine.
They are rightly joined: for whoever, abstaining, hates
wine, will feel no help from the goddess.
Why do you trouble me, branches? I am Pallas's tree:
take these clusters away from here. The virgin flees Bromius [Bacchus].
Father Bacchus: what mortal eye has known you?
And whose skilled hand shaped your limbs?
Praxiteles, who saw me carrying off the Cnossian girl [Ariadne].
And he depicted me just as I was at that time.
Why are you young, and why does your beard still bloom
with tender down, when in years you could surpass the old man of Pylos [Nestor]?
If you ever learn to be sparing with my gifts,
you too will always be younger, and strong of heart.
You have timbrels in your hands, horns on your head.
Whom (but madmen) do such signs befit?
This I teach: he who abuses my gift takes on
horns, and, maddened, shakes the soft sistra.
What does that almost fiery colour on your limbs mean? (may this omen
be averted) — are you yourself burning on mortal pyres?
When my father [Jupiter] drew me from Semele's womb with fire-spewing
lightning, he plunged me, stained with ash, into the waters.
Hence he is wise who dilutes us well with flowing waters:
who does not scorch his liver with burning fire.
But now teach me, in what way do you wish to be mixed? And by what
rule can a sound man safely take hold of you?
Let him add a quarter of water, who desires to have drunk
a cup of Falernian: it is pleasing for cups to be taken this way.
Stay within the heminae: for he who tries to go
further — is lively at first, but soon, drunk, runs wild.
This is too hard a thing. Throats slope downward, sweetly
you flow. Alas, no advantage comes easily.
The fathers [senators] granted Fabius a grass crown,
because by delay he had broken the Carthaginians and Hannibal.
The lark hides her nest for herself in bent grass,
commonly they say she thus keeps her chicks warm.
Sacred to Saturn and Mars is the herb which Glaucus,
son of Polybus, ate, and is believed to have become a god.
By these knots, protection and safety are rightly signified:
and this finger-grass has so many powers.

27.motto: To harm no one by word or deed.

reading: She pursues and keeps watch on the footsteps of men, Nemesis,
and holds in her hand a measuring cubit and hard reins.
Lest you do anything evil, or speak wicked words —
she commands that measure be present in all things.

28.motto: At last, at last justice prevails.

reading: The shield of the descendant of Aeacus [Achilles], drenched with Hector's blood,
which the unjust assembly of the Greeks gave to the Ithacan [Ulysses]:
Neptune, more just, seized it when it was cast into the sea
by shipwreck, so it might reach its own master.
For the wave carried it to Ajax's tomb on the shore,
which roars, and strikes the tomb with such a voice:
'You have won, son of Telamon, you are more worthy of the arms.
It is right for favour to yield to justice.'
After Roman eloquence, with Cicero slain,
the bitter plague of his country had destroyed it,
Antony, victorious, mounted a chariot, and yoked lions,
and forced their necks to bow beneath the harsh yoke,
wishing by this riddle to signify that great-hearted
leaders had yielded to his arms.
The stork, noted for piety in her airy nest,
warms her unfledged chicks, dear pledges.
And she expects such gifts to be returned to her in kind,
whenever, an aged mother, she will need this help.
Nor does the pious offspring fail that hope, but carries the weary
bodies of its parents on its shoulders, and offers food by beak.
On one side of the marble column on tombs stands
a pitcher, on the other a washbasin is to be seen.
This form reminds us that justice was administered without corruption,
and that the deceased kept clean hands.

32.motto: The good have nothing to fear from the rich.

reading: Marius, joined to me by a common wall, and also
Subbardus — names well known in our forum —
being rich in money, are building, and strive even further,
alas, to block my windows on every side.
Wretched me: like Phineus, the twin
Harpies seize me, to drive me from my own home —
unless my integrity, and my spirit, seeker of what is honourable,
be a Zetes to them, be a Calais to them.
What cause moves you, Saturnian bird, that you
perch, lofty, on the tomb of great Aristomenes?
This I tell you: as much as I surpass other birds in strength,
so much does Aristomenes surpass the demigods.
Let timid doves settle on the tombs of the timid,
we eagles grant favourable signs to the fearless.
And sad fortune must be patiently borne by man,
and excessive good fortune has often been a thing to fear.
'Endure,' Epictetus used to say, 'and abstain.' One must
suffer much, and keep one's hands from what is forbidden.
Thus the bull, bound at the right hock, bears the herdsman's
command: thus it restrains itself from the pregnant cows.

35.motto: On one who knows not how to flatter.

reading: You wish to know why the Thessalian land so often
changes masters, and seeks to have various leaders:
it does not know how to flatter, or thrust false caresses on anyone,
a custom which every royal court possesses.
But, like a spirited horse, it throws from its back
any rider who does not know how to manage it.
Yet the master too may not rage: his only
revenge is to order the wild one to wear harsher bits.
The palm strains against weight, and bends into an arch —
the more it is pressed, the more it lifts the burden:
it also bears fragrant, sweet dates,
to which the first honour among the table's delicacies is given.
Go, boy, and climbing on its branches gather these: whoever
is of steadfast mind will carry off worthy rewards.

37.motto: I carry all my things with me.

reading: The poor Hun, most wretched dweller by the Scythian sea,
his limbs livid, scorched by perpetual frost.
He who knows not the riches of Ceres, nor the gifts of Lyaeus [Bacchus],
yet always has precious coverings:
for pelts of mice wrap him on every side.
Only his eyes lie open, all else he keeps covered.
Thus he fears no thief, thus he scorns winds and rains;
safe among men, and safe among gods.
A wondrous concord reigns among crows in their life,
and mutual, unbroken faith stands among them.
Hence these sceptres bear birds: for, clearly, all
leaders stand and fall by the consent of the people:
if you remove this from their midst, headlong
discord rushes in, and drags with it the fates of kingdoms.
When Rome was readying leaders for civil war,
and the warlike land was falling by its own forces:
it was the custom, when troops joined the same side,
for joined right hands to be given as a mutual gift.
This is the form of alliance: this is the sign of Concord,
that those whom love joins, hands too should join.
Among the triplet brothers there was concord.
Such mutual devotion together, and a single love:
that, unconquered by human strength, they held
vast kingdoms, called by the one name of Geryon.

41.motto: One can do nothing, two can do very much.

reading: The son of Laertes, and together with him the son of Tydeus,
the skilled hand of Zenalis rendered in this wax.
The one excels in strength, the other is strong in sharpness of mind,
yet neither is without need of the other's help.
When the two come joined together, victory is certain.
Alone, it is mind, or else the right hand, that fails a man.
Though Ocean, father of waves, should rouse all his billows,
and though you, barbarous Turk, should drink the whole Danube dry,
still you will not burst in by breaking the frontier, while Caesar
Charles gives the signals of war to the peoples.
So sacred oaks stand firm upon their roots,
though the winds shake their dry leaves.
Our republic is driven by countless storms,
and only the hope of coming salvation remains:
no different from a ship in the midst of the sea, which
the winds sweep along, and which already gapes from the salt waters.
But if the shining stars, the brothers of Helen, should come:
good hope restores the spirits that were lost.
What goddess gazes up at the stars with so joyful a face?
Whose brush rendered this image?
The hands of Elpidius made it. I am the one called
Good Hope, who offers ready help to the wretched.
Why is your mantle green? Because, with me as guide, all things flourish.
Why do you carry in your hands the broken weapons of death?
Because it is fitting for the living to hope; from the buried I cut hope off.
Why do you sit idle on the lid of a little cask?
I alone stayed at home, while harms flew about on every side,
as the revered muse of the old man of Ascra [Hesiod] taught.
What bird is with you? The crow, most faithful of omen-birds,
who, when she cannot say "it is well," says "it will be."
Who are your companions? Good Outcome, and headlong Cupid.
Who go before you? They are called the vain dreams of the waking.
Who stands joined beside you? The Rhamnusian avenger of crimes [Nemesis],
so that, of course, you may hope for nothing but what is permitted.
A client brought me the snout of a bristly boar for the new year,
"take this," he said, "as a gift for your belly."
It always moves forward, and never looks back,
when, greedy, it roots up the grass with its curved snout.
Men have the same care, that hope, once it has slipped,
should not fall backward: and that what lies further on should also be better.

46.motto: One must not hope for what is forbidden.

reading: Hope and Nemesis stand together at our altars,
so that, of course, you may hope for nothing but what is permitted.
If the master's wife defiles the house with adultery,
the Porphyrio bird loses heart, and perishes from grief.
The cause lies hidden in nature's secrets. Let this bird be
a sure sign of pure chastity.

48.motto: On a victory won by trickery.

reading: I, Virtue, bathe the tomb of Ajax with tears.
Alas, wretched, my white hair torn.
This indeed still remained: that I should be defeated by a Greek judge,
and that deceit should prevail over the better cause.
A small lizard, its body starred with black spots —
the Stellio, which dwells in hiding-places and hollow tombs,
bears, spotted, the emblems of envy and wicked deceit.
Alas, too well known to jealous young wives.
For whoever drinks wine in which a Stellio has been steeped
has her face covered with an ugly blemish.
Hence frequent revenge, the mistress deceived through wine,
whom, once the flower of her beauty is lost, the lover abandons.
A fattened decoy duck, with dark-blue feathers,
accustomed to fly out and return to its masters.
Seeing kindred flocks flying through the air,
she calls out, and slips into their flock,
until she leads the unwary beneath the outstretched nets.
The captured ones clamor, but she, knowing all, stays silent.
The treacherous bird stains herself with kindred blood,
helpful to others, ruinous to her own kind.
They say that wasps carved from marble are on Archilochus' tomb,
sure emblems of an evil tongue.
A band of robbers and thieves, Scaeva, goes with you
through the city as a companion: a troop girded with dread swords.
And so you, spendthrift, think yourself generous-minded,
because your cauldron lures many evil men.
Behold a new Actaeon, who, having taken on horns,
gave himself up as prey to his own dogs.
Always it gapes, always drawing in and out the thin air on which it feeds,
the Chameleon.
And it changes its face, taking on various colors,
except red, or white.
So too the Flatterer feeds on popular favor,
and, gaping, devours everything.
And he imitates only the dark habits of his prince,
unacquainted with what is white and chaste.

54.motto: One who has once squandered his own should not be trusted with another's.

reading: Why do you pile your nest in the lap of the Colchian woman [Medea]? Alas,
unwitting bird, why do you so ill entrust your chicks?
The dread mother Medea, most savage, destroyed
her own children — and do you hope that she will spare yours?
He is swept headlong, and in vain the charioteer tightens the reins,
carried by a horse unbridled in mouth.
You would hardly trust such a man, whom no reason governs,
and who is rashly led by his own whim.
The shield bears the painted face of a raging lion,
and on its upper edge has an inscribed verse:
"This is the terror of men, whose possessor is the son of Atreus" —
such were the emblems the great-hearted Agamemnon bore.
You see Phaethon, charioteer of his father's chariot,
who dared to steer the fire-breathing horses of the Sun.
Who, after he scattered the greatest conflagrations over the earth,
rashly fell, wretched, from the chariot he had mounted.
So many kings, borne by Fortune's wheels toward the stars,
whom youthful ambition drives on:
after great ruin both to mankind and to themselves,
at last pay the penalty for all their crimes.

58.motto: Against those who dare anything beyond their strength.

reading: While he sleeps, while he refreshes his body with sweet slumber,
beneath a pine, holding his club and his other weapons,
the band of Pygmies thinks it can lay Alcides [Hercules]
low in death: poorly aware of its own strength.
Roused, he himself crushes the enemy like fleas,
and carries them off, wrapped up in the fierce lion's hide.
You wash an Ethiopian — why in vain? Ah, stop.
No one can illuminate the darkness of black night.
Why do many call countryfolk, a rustic race, "cuckoos"?
What cause has been given for this?
The cuckoo sings in early spring, at the time when whoever
has not finished [pruning] his vines is rightly called lazy.
It lays its eggs in others' nests, just like that man
whose marriage-bed his wife betrays by adultery.
That he took his name from the winged daughter of Minyas (Meneis)
is what the writers report of Socrates' follower Chaerephon.
The man had a dark face and a shrill little voice;
by such a mark this man could be branded.
The creature that flies only at evening, that is half-blind in daylight,
that, though it bears wings, in all else is like a mouse,
is applied to different things. First, it signifies bad debtors,
who lie low and fear the court.
Then also philosophers, who, while seeking the things of heaven,
grow dim-eyed and see only what is false.
Finally also the cunning, who secretly follow both sides,
gain trust from neither side.
The ancients called the lion's tail 'alcaea' [Greek ἀλκαία, from ἀλκή, 'strength'],
stirred by it, the lion conceives grave wrath.
When the yellow bile rises, and the pain grows raw
with black bile, it stirs up untamed fury.

64.motto: Against him who prepares harm for himself.

reading: The goat says: not willingly do I now suckle the wolf with my udder,
for the shepherd's ill-judged foresight commands it.
Once he has grown, after my udders he will feed on me.
Wickedness is bent by no kindness.
You wonder that in our verse you are called 'Otus,'
though your name from your forebears has long been 'Otho.'
The bird is eared, and has feathers like the owl,
and the skilled fowler catches it as it dances.
Hence we call fools, easily caught, 'oti' [owls] —
bear this fitting name yourself too.
When the hungry lynx eats its food,
and out of hunger devours the captured fawn,
if it happens to look elsewhere, or turns its eyes away,
forgetting the food it holds right there in its claw,
it goes seeking some uncertain prey (so great is its forgetfulness).
He who foolishly neglects his own, seeks another's.
Behold a statue made from a statue, marble drawn from marble —
insolent Niobe, who dared to compare herself with the gods.
Pride is a woman's vice, and it betrays
a hardness of face and feelings like those found in stone.
Down to the hips a woman, girdled below with the barking whelps
of monsters, Scylla was two-formed.
The monsters are taken to be avarice, boldness, plunder.
But Scylla is anyone who has no shame in his face.
Because your own beauty pleased you too much, Narcissus,
it was turned into a flower, a plant known for its stupefying power.
Self-love (Philautia) is the withering of talent, a ruin that has
destroyed, and goes on destroying, many learned men:
who, having cast aside the method of the ancients, seek new doctrines,
and have nothing to hand down but their own fancies.
Why, chattering Procne, do you break my morning sleep,
and sing, bird of Daulis, with your clamorous mouth?
Tereus deserved to become the hoopoe, for he chose only to prune with the sword
rather than tear out by the root that immoderate tongue.
A filthy woman, eating viper's flesh,
whose eyes ache, and who devours her own heart,
whom leanness and pallor possess, and who carries in her hand a thorny
weapon — thus is Envy depicted.
Goat-footed Faunus, his temples wreathed with rocket,
bears sure symbols of immoderate lust.
Rocket is lustful, and the goat is the sign of lechery,
and satyrs are always wont to love nymphs.
On airy cliffs, on the edge of the highest rock,
a bitter fig tree bears harsh fruits,
which crows eat, which the shameless crow devours —
fruits that have no human usefulness at all.
So parasites and whores enjoy the wealth of fools:
while it brings honest men no benefit at all.
What tomb is this? Whose urn? It is that of Ephyraean Lais. Ah, did
Fate not blush to destroy such great beauty?
There was no beauty left by then: age had already worn her down,
already the wary old woman had dedicated her mirror to Venus.
What does the carved ram mean, which a lioness holds,
gripped by its hind part with her claws?
Because she herself held her captured lovers no differently:
the ram is the husband of the flock; the lover is held by the haunch.
The fisherman, dressed in the shaggy hide of a she-goat,
having set two horns upon his own head,
standing at the very edge of the shore, deceives the love-struck Sargus:
the fish whom passion for the snub-nosed flock drives into the snares.
The goat stands for the harlot, the Sargus becomes like the lover,
who, wretched, perishes, caught by shameful love.
So great, they say, was the power of Circe, daughter of the Sun,
that she turned many men into strange monsters.
Witness Picus, tamer of horses, then two-formed Scylla,
and the swine, after the Ithacan's men had drunk her wine.
Circe, by her famous name, signifies a courtesan,
and that whoever loves loses the reason of his mind.
Cypris laid the lifeless Adonis, his groin
pierced by the fierce tusk, among lettuce leaves.
Hence lettuce resists the generative power as much
as lustful rocket can scarcely stir it.
Lest fierce love conquer you, or any woman
tear your mind apart with magical arts,
let the Bacchic bird, the wryneck, be made ready for you,
which you should set four-spoked within the ring of a wheel:
so that with beak and tail, and its two wings folded together,
it forms a cross — such will be an amulet against every spell.
It is said that by this sign of Venus, Pagasaean Jason
could not be harmed by the Phasian tricks.
The white creature is believed to signify delights
and softness, but the reason for this is not quite clear to me.
Is it because its nature is lustful, and its desire great?
Or because it adorns Roman brides with its fur?
Many call the Sarmatian creature 'sable,'
and the Arabian musk is famed for its sweet fragrance.
The Essene sits idle on the bushel and gazes at the stars,
and underneath he covers the torch lit with fire.
Sloth, under the guise of righteousness, veiled by a cowl,
helps neither itself nor others in any way.
Let every idler go away. For to settle one's seat on the grain-measure,
the sacred precepts of the old Samian [Pythagoras] forbid us.
Rise, then, and accustom your hands to hard labor,
that the morrow's hour may give you measured food.

82.motto: Against those who easily fall away from virtue.

reading: Small as a slug, the fish Remora, scorning the force of wind
and of oars, alone can bring a ship to a halt.
So, too, some who are borne toward the stars by talent and virtue
are held back midway by a trifling cause:
such is an anxious lawsuit, or the whorish passion
that calls young men away from noble studies.
That the little starry heron [bittern] reproduces the pursuits and habits
of the idle servant was an old tale.
It was this tale that invented how the servant Asterias took on the shape of the bird;
let the vouching for it rest with the historians.
This bird is like a degenerate falcon that flutters about in the air,
and the ancient poets called it 'ardelio' [a busy idler].
Alas, wretched Tantalus stands thirsting amid the waters,
and, hungering, cannot reach the fruit so near.
Change but the name, and the same will be said of you, miser,
who, as if you had nothing, do not enjoy what you have.
Septitius, richest of all men,
no old man holds broader fields than he.
Cheating his own appetite, and his tables ready-laid,
he eats nothing but beets and tough turnips.
To whom shall I liken him, whom abundance makes poor?
To a donkey? Even so: he bears its very likeness.
For the donkey carries costly provisions on its back,
yet feeds itself, poor creature, on brambles or tough sedge.
The vain court that rears its Palatine followers
is said to bind them with gilded fetters.
Which with its beak (as with a clyster) washes out its own bowel —
the ibis, known on the shores of the Nile —
has passed into a term of reproach: by which Publius
Naso [Ovid] calls his enemy, and Battiades [Callimachus] his own.

88.motto: Against those who grow rich from the public's harm.

reading: Whoever catches eels, if he sweeps clear
rivers, if he dares approach unmuddied lakes,
will come away empty, and waste his labor; let him then stir up
much chalky silt, and let his little blade churn the glassy waters:
he will grow rich. So a troubled commonwealth is profit for those
who, constrained by the laws in peacetime, go hungry.

89.motto: Against the avaricious, or those to whom strangers offer a better lot.

reading: Seated upon the dolphin, Arion furrows the blue waters,
and with this song charms its ears, and bridles its mouth with sound.
The mind of beasts is not so fierce as that of a greedy man:
we who are seized by men are rescued by fish.
A man is painted with a crane's throat and a swollen belly,
who carries in his hands a gull, or a pelican.
Such was the shape of Dionysius, and such of Apicius,
and of those whom dainty gluttony makes renowned.

91.motto: The image of Ocnus. Concerning those who give to harlots what ought to be put to good use.

reading: Tireless, he does not cease to twist a rope of broom-fibre,
and to join the damp threads with a skilled hand.
But however much the diligent man scarcely twists in many hours,
the little she-ass of an idle belly devours at once.
Woman, an idle creature, snatches the gains heaped up by her easygoing husband,
and squanders them on her own finery.
Accept these river crabs which we give you:
such gifts suit your character.
They have watchful eyes, and many rows armed
with claws like shears, and a very great belly.
So, too, you have a belly thrust forward with fat paunch,
and swift feet, and spines fitted to the foot.
When you wander about the crossroads, and roam round the places at table,
and hurl biting, false jibes at others.

93.motto: A small kitchen does not suffice for two gluttons.

reading: In modest means there is nothing one can gain: and a single
bush does not feed two robins.

epigrams.label: ANOTHER.
reading: In slender means there is no hope of gain: and on one
bush two figpeckers do not perch well together.

94.motto: A captive on account of gluttony.

reading: The ruler of the larder, and gnawer of his master's table,
the mouse spied oysters gaping open at the edges of their lips.
Setting his soft whiskers against them, he bit the deceptive bones,
but these, once touched, suddenly shut their house.
And they held the caught thief in a foul prison —
he who had given himself into a dark tomb.
It bellows with a fierce voice, has an overly wide throat, its beak
resembles a nose, and a trumpet full of holes.
It will mark a deformed pettifogger, given over to belly
and gullet, when the bird 'truo' is painted.
It is an old custom that professors
have certain extra nicknames attached to them.
He who explains only easy and open passages
is called Curtius 'the Rule' [Canon].
He who turns over the same ground, and repeats too much,
[is called] 'Meander,' as was Parisius.
Obscure and confused, as Picus was,
will be named 'the Labyrinth.'
Too brief, cutting much away, as Claudius,
will bear the nickname 'the Point' [Mucro].
He who even breaks columns with his voice, Parpalus,
is called by the students 'the Bellower' [Truo].
On the contrary, Albius was named, because his voice was thin,
'the Bat.'
But he who maims the last syllables, cut short,
Crassus is called 'the Swallow.'
But he who, as a clipper [colobotes], maims the final syllables,
is like the starling in the proverb.
This one lisps, that one is hoarse, another chatters on.
This one hisses like a viper.
That one makes an uproar with gaping mouth and nostrils.
For this one, the tongue works like a drill.
Another hiccups, and coughs, hesitating.
Another sputters like a fine rain.
As many vices as act upon human affairs,
just as many names arise.
Nations worship Pan (that is to say, the nature of things),
a half-goat man, and a half-man god.
He is man as far as the groin, because the innate virtue in us,
rising from the heart, sits in the lofty citadel of the head.
Below that he is a goat, because nature propagates us through the ages
by copulation: as it does birds, scaly creatures, brutes, and wild beasts.
As for what we share with other living creatures, the goat is the token
of lust, and openly bears the marks of Venus.
Some have attributed wisdom to the heart, others to the brain.
No measure, nor any reason, governs the lower parts.
As Fortune stands upon a sphere, so Hermes sits upon a cube:
he presides over the arts, she over various chances.
Art was made against the power of Fortune: but art itself
often needs help when fortune is bad.
Learn then good arts, studious youth,
which carry with them the benefits of a sure lot.
Both sons of Jupiter, both tender and beardless,
the one whom Latona bore, and the one whom Semele bore,
hail, and flourish together in eternal youth;
by your divine will, may it be long-lasting for me too.
You with wine wash away cares, you with diet wash away ailments,
that late old age may approach with lagging step.

100.motto: On the four seasons of the year.

reading: The finch, a bird, announces that winter has come.
To us, in new spring, the chattering swallow returns.
The cuckoo signals that summer is to be expected.
Only in autumn are the figpeckers to be seen.
Receive this crater of Nestor with its twin bases,
a work poured out from a heavy mass of silver.
Little studs of gold; around it stand four handles:
on each one sits a tawny dove.
Only long-lived Nestor could lift it.
Would you explain what the Muse of Maeonides [Homer] means?
The cup itself is the sky: its colour is silver:
the golden studs are the stars of heaven.
They think the doves he spoke of are the Pleiades.
The twin bosses are the greater and the lesser beast.
This Nestor, wise from long experience, understands:
the brave wage wars, the clever one holds the stars.

102.motto: What is above us is nothing to us.

reading: Prometheus, hanging forever on the rock of Caucasus,
is torn — the claw of the sacred bird rips out his liver.
And he wishes he had not made man: hating the modellers of clay,
he curses the torch kindled from the stolen fire.
The hearts of the wise are gnawed by many cares,
who strive to know the ways of heaven and the doings of the gods.
Icarus, who was carried through the heights and the air, until
the melted wax cast you headlong into the sea —
now the same wax, and the burning fire, raise you up again,
that by your own example you may teach sure doctrines.
Let the astrologer beware of predicting anything: headlong —
for likewise [?] the impostor [falls], while he flies above the stars.

104.motto: Those who gaze at the heights, fall.

reading: While he tricks the thrushes with birdlime, and the larks with a snare,
and the arrow he lets fly strikes the high-flying crane,
the fowler, unwary, treads with his foot on a dipsas: she, avenging
the harm, spits forth the venom from her mouth.
So perishes he who, bow drawn, gazes up at the stars,
heedless of the fate that lies right before his feet.

105.motto: Love is the most powerful passion.

reading: Behold how the unconquered charioteer overcomes the lion's strength —
the little boy Love, carved on the gem:
how with this hand he holds the whip, with that he turns the reins,
and how much beauty is in the boy's face.
May dire plague be far from us: he who is able
to conquer such a beast — will he hold back his hand from us?
Naked Love — do you see how he smiles, and gazes calmly?
He has neither torches nor a bow whose horns he might bend.
But in one hand he holds flowers, in the other a fish,
as if to give his laws both to the land and to the sea.
The winged god broke the winged thunderbolt, showing
that Love is a fire stronger than fire.

108.motto: On a scholar captured by Love.

reading: Immersed in studies, expert in expounding the law,
and the greatest of bookmen,
he loves Helianira more than the Thracian
prince ever loved the rival of her own sister.
Why, Cypris, did you surpass Pallas before another judge?
Is it not enough to have won on Ida?

109.motto: Ἀντέρως, id amor virtutis ("Anteros, that is, the love of virtue").

reading: Tell me, where are your curved bows? where are the arrows, Cupid,
with which you are wont to pierce the soft hearts of youths?
Where is the gloomy torch? where the wings? why does your hand
bear three garlands? why do your temples wear yet another?
"I have nothing to do (stranger) with the common Cypris,
nor has any form of pleasure carried me away,
but I kindle in the pure minds of men the fires
of learning: I draw souls up to the lofty stars.
Out of Virtue herself I weave four garlands,
and of these the one that is Wisdom's, the foremost, covers my temples."

greek.translation: Anteros, that is, the love of virtue.

110.motto: Ἀντέρως, Amor virtutis, alium Cupidinem superans ("Anteros, the love of virtue, surpassing the other Cupid").

reading: Winged, and hostile to the winged Love, Nemesis painted him,
taming bow with bow, and fires with fire.
So that he might suffer what he did to others. But this boy, who once
bore his weapons fearlessly, now, wretched, weeps.
Thrice he spits deep into his bosom, and (a wondrous thing) fire
is burned by fire: Love hates the furies of Love.

greek.original: Αντέρως, Amor virtutis, alium Cupidinem superans.
greek.translation: Anteros, the love of virtue, surpassing the other Cupid.

reading: Having left his mother far behind, the Lydian child
had withdrawn a little way: but you, dire bees, carried him off.
He had come to you, thinking you gentle birds,
though even a fierce viper would not be so cruel.
Ah, you give stings in return for the sweet gift of honey.
Alas the pain! Without you, no joy at all is given.
While he was stealing honey from the hives, the wicked bee stung
thieving Love, and left her sting on the tips
of his fingers: and the boy groans, fretting over his swollen fingertip.
And wandering about, he stamps the ground: and shows Venus
his pain, and gravely complains that a little bee,
so small a creature, could inflict such harmful wounds.
To whom Venus, laughing, said: "You too, my son, resemble
this beast: small as you are, you deal so many harmful wounds."
Who Love is, many poets of old have sung,
telling of his deeds under various names.
In this they agree: that he lacks clothing, that he is small of body.
Bearing weapons and wings, he has no eyes.
Such is his face, such the guise of the god. But if I may say so
against such great bards, I think a falsehood lies beneath this.
Why should he go about naked? As though a god lacked cloaks,
he who possesses all the riches of the conquered world.
Or how, I ask, could he, naked, escape the snows and the Alpine
north wind, and meadows bound by frost?
If he is a boy, do you call him a boy who outlasts Nestor?
Or do you not know the learned songs of the old man of Ascra?
A boy is fickle, but this one is stubborn: once he has entered
hearts, he can never leave them of his own will.
But he carries a quiver and arrows — why this useless burden?
Can an infant manage to bend the hard horns of a bow?
Why does he have wings, which he does not know how to carry into the sky?
He has no skill to aim his shafts at the livers of birds.
He creeps along the ground, and forever wounds the mortal
hearts of men: yet, turned to stone, he never stirs his wings.
If he is blind, and wears a band, what use is a blindfold
to a blind man? Does he therefore see any less?
And who would believe him an archer, deprived of sight?
An ordinary blind man's shafts fly at random, but his are sure.
They say he is fiery, and turns flames within his breast.
Why then does he still live? Fire devours everything.
And why, moreover, is he not quenched by swelling waves,
as often as he enters the soft hearts of the Naiads?
But you, lest you be caught in such great errors, listen:
our verses will tell what true Love is.
He is a pleasant labor amid playful leisure. His sign
is a Punic fruit upon a black shield.
Having long since left your homeland, and forgotten your own,
whom either blood or love provided you,
you dwell in Rome: nor does any care to return home ever come over you.
Only the honor of the eternal city holds you captive.
So the advance band of Ithacans, seduced by the sweetness of the lotus,
had abandoned both their homeland and their leader.
Birds without wings, and maidens without legs,
fish without a beak, which nevertheless sing with their mouths:
who would believe any such creatures exist? Nature has refused to join such things,
but the Sirens teach that it could be done.
It is a forbidden thing, this woman who ends in a dark fish,
because lust carries with it very many monsters.
By looks, by words, by purity of soul, men are drawn —
Parthenope, Ligia, and Leucosia.
These the Muses strip of their feathers, and these Ulysses outwits.
Clearly, the learned have nothing to do with a harlot.

116.motto: An old man in love with a girl.

reading: While Sophocles (though of advanced age) draws the girl
Archippe, a courtesan, to his desires,
and entices her with payment too, the mad young men bore it ill
out of jealousy, and marked both of them with this verse:
"As the owl sits upon tombs, and the horned owl over corpses,
so our girl sits with Sophocles."
Dun-brown is the sign of sorrow: we all
wear this garb when we give offerings at tombs.
But the robe of a sincere spirit and a pure mind is white.
Hence linen cloth is dear to sacred men.
Green teaches us to hope. Hope is said to dwell in green,
as often as, disappointed, it falls back in vain.
Yellow is the color of the greedy, and suits lovers too,
and harlots, and those whose hope has proved sure.
But let red clothing adorn armed knights,
and let it mark the blush of modesty in boys.
Sky-blue suits sailors, and those seers who, awestruck,
seek heavenly things out of excessive piety.
Cheap and plain are fleeces of dun-pale cloaks:
such coverings as the wooden-shod are wont to have.
Whoever is tormented by great cares, or by jealousy in love,
is thought not ill covered by a tawny garment.
Let whoever is content with his lot wear violet,
and bear the weariness of Fortune with equanimity.
As nature is varied in producing colors,
so one suits one man, another another: but each has his own taste.
The caduceus, entwined with serpents, with twin wings,
stands upright between the horns of Amalthea.
Thus it shows how men mighty in mind and skilled in speech
are blessed by a great abundance of riches.
After he was defeated by Caesar's soldiery, and saw
Pharsalia awash with civil blood,
already about to drive the blade into his dying breast,
Brutus spoke these words with a bold mouth:
"Unhappy Virtue, provident only in words,
why do you follow Fortune as your mistress in deeds?"

120.motto: Poverty harms the greatest talents, preventing their advancement.

reading: My right hand holds a stone: my other hand bears up wings.
As the feather lifts me, so the heavy weight drags me down.
By talent I could have flown through the highest citadels,
had not envious poverty weighed me down.
This is the work of Lysippus, whose homeland is Sicyon. Who are you?
— The pivot of time once seized, mastering all things.
Why do you stand on wings? — I am forever whirling. Why do you keep
winged sandals on your feet? — The light breeze sweeps me everywhere.
Why is there a slender razor in your right hand, tell me? — This sign
teaches that I am sharper than any blade.
Why the lock of hair on your forehead? — So I may be seized as I come to meet you. But you there,
tell me, why is the back of your head bald?
So that, once someone lets the winged one go,
I cannot be caught again by grasping my hair.
With such art the craftsman made me, stranger, for your sake,
and so that I may warn everyone: I stand in an open portico.
Seeing the ranks flee in a scattered column,
‘Who now blows into my horns?’ says Faunus.

123.motto: Against those who praise things unworthy of praise.

reading: The huge hordes of the Galatians, with his half-armed soldiery,
trembling Antiochus had routed, beyond his hope,
when the fierce force of the Lucanian oxen [elephants], the fury of their trunks,
then for the first time had seized the enemy's horses.
So, setting up a trophy, he painted on it the image of an elephant,
and said besides: ‘we would have perished along with our allies,
had not this most hideous beast, the elephant, saved us.’
As it is pleasing to have won, so it is shameful to have won thus.
The Gourd is said to have grown up beside the lofty pine,
and to have flourished with abundant foliage.
Having wound about its branches, and risen above the very top,
it believed itself superior to the other trees.
The pine replied: too brief is this glory. For soon
winter will come upon you and destroy you cruelly.
While with savage weapons they rushed to wound each other,
the lioness fierce with claw, the boar fearsome with tusk,
the vulture runs up to watch, and seizes its meal.
The victor's glory will become its future prey.

126.motto: One must begin under good auspices.

reading: A thing begun under ill auspices does not know how to turn out well.
Things done under a lucky omen prosper.
Whatever you are doing, if a weasel crosses your path, abandon it;
this wicked beast bears the signs of an evil fate.
This indeed was still lacking, after so many ills, at last, for our
fields — that the locusts should carry off whatever was left in them.
We saw countless swarms advancing with the East wind as their leader,
such as not even Attila's hordes, nor Xerxes' camps, ever were.
These devoured all the hay, the millet, the grain,
and hope is in straits, unless prayers are left to us.
The gluttonous kite, whom nausea from excessive food had tormented,
says: ‘woe is me, mother, my own guts are pouring from my mouth.’
But she replies: ‘why do you weep? why do you believe these are your own guts,
you who, living by plunder, vomit up nothing but what is another's?’
Three girls of equal age were once playing
at lots: to see which of them would go first to the Stygian waters.
But the one for whom the cast die had fallen out badly
laughed, blind girl, at her own lot.
When suddenly, struck on the head by a collapsing roof, she died,
and paid the debt owed to her reckless jest.
In adverse matters, ill fortune is not mistaken; but in
fortunate ones, there is room neither for prayers nor for the hand [effort].
After Jupiter cast Ate down from the heavenly seats,
— alas, how grievous the harm with which she torments men!
She flies swiftly on her feet and on swift wings,
and leaves nothing untouched by misfortunes.
Therefore the Litae, offspring of Jupiter, accompany her as she goes,
ready to mend whatever ill she will have done.
But because they are slow of foot, one-eyed, and weary with age,
they restore nothing except afterward, after a long time.
The sparrow had entrusted its pledges [its young] to the branches of the plane tree,
and well it would have been, had they not been seen by a fierce serpent.
This one swallowed all the chicks, and the wretched parent too,
then itself turned to stone, worthy to perish by such a death.
These, unless Calchas lies, are monuments of a long labor,
whose fame shall endure forever.

132.motto: Immortality is acquired through the pursuit of letters.

reading: Neptune's trumpeter, whose lowest part is a sea-monster,
while his face shows him to be a god of the sea:
Triton is enclosed within the circle of a serpent,
which holds its own tail gripped in its mouth.
Fame follows men distinguished in spirit, and glorious deeds,
and bids that they be read throughout the whole world.

133.motto: The tomb of Giovanni Galeazzo Visconti, first Duke of Milan.

reading: In place of a tomb, set up Italy, set up arms, and captains,
and the sea, which roars as far as its twin gulfs.
Add to these the barbarian force vainly trying to break in,
and troops bought for pay for savage wars.
The serpent-bearer, standing at the very summit, might say:
‘Who has set me, so great, above such small things?’

greek.where: engraving inscription (ribbon around the serpent, Greek, partly mirrored/inverted)
greek.note: greek[].reading is null in the source — the ribbon text is illegible/not normalized at the transcription stage; no translation given.

reading: While Thrasybulus was freeing his homeland with just arms,
and bidding every man lay aside his feuds,
the whole united order, as if for a great gift, gave him
a wreath of Pallas's leaf [the olive] to wear.
Bind your hair, Thrasybulus, bear this honor alone;
in this great city no one rivals you.

135.motto: The undying name of the valiant.

reading: You see the tomb of the grandson of Aeacus [Achilles] on the Rhoetean shore,
which white Thetis often visits on foot.
This stone is always covered with green amaranth,
because the hero's honor shall never die.
Here lies the bulwark of the Greeks, the slayer of great Hector. He owes
no more to Homer than Homer owes to him.
A golden clasp used to fasten the garments of the Cecropians [Athenians]:
to which a cicada, clinging by its 'tooth', was attached.
The shoe beneath which, in Arcadian fashion, lay a crescent,
the mullea [red shoe], is worn by the fathers, sons of Romulus:
because, claiming to be native-born, men illustrious by ancient nobility
bore these signs.
Eloquence surpasses the praises of unconquered strength:
it unravels the words of the Sophists and their empty snares.
No fury or madness is more powerful than virtue.
Wealth yields to the wise man for his steady perseverance.
He scorns greed, and takes no joy in plunder or usury.
He conquers, and strips effeminate deeds of their honors.
He purges filth, and adds refinement to minds.
He hates unlawful unions, and drives away the guilty.
Barbarism and impious savagery pay the penalty at last.
The valor of one man scatters the massed enemy.
He brings into his homeland very many goods from foreign shores.
He flies through the learned mouths of men, and never dies.
Bastards, always celebrate the honors of Hercules:
for he was the first of your order.
Nor could he become a god, before, as an infant, he sucked
the milk which Juno, unaware of the deceit, gave him.
As the falcon, flying aloft, cleaves the thin air,
while the jackdaw, the goose, and the duck feed on the ground:
so the mighty Pindar climbs to the very heights above the ether,
so Bacchylides knows only how to crawl upon the ground.
Because you have stained your fine beginnings with a shameful end,
and have turned your duty into harm,
you have done what the goat does: the pail of her own milk,
when she kicks it, and with her hoof spills her own wealth.
The kite — of baser stock — follows the high-flying harpa,
and often gets a share of the falling prey.
The sargus follows the mullet, and the food it has scorned
and passed by, it greedily devours with its mouth.
So Oenocrates deals with me: but the students' lecture hall that I have left
makes use of this bleary-eyed man as of a bleary eye.

142.motto: Albutius to Alciato, advising him to withdraw from the Italian turmoils and to teach in France.

reading: The tree that gave these fruits, a stranger to our sky,
came earlier from the eastern realm of Persia:
by being transplanted it became better: once harmful
in its homeland, here it bears sweet fruit for us.
It bears a leaf like a tongue, bears fruit most like a heart —
from this, Alciato, learn to lead your life.
Far from your homeland you will be held in greater worth:
you are greatly wise in heart, and no less strong in speech.

143.motto: The prince providing for the safety of his subjects.

reading: As often as the Titan-born brothers [the winds] trouble the seas,
the cast anchor then helps the wretched sailors.
The dolphin, friendly to men, wraps around it, so that
it may be fixed more securely in the deep shoals.
How fitting it is for kings to bear this emblem, mindful
that they are to their own people what the anchor is to sailors!

144.motto: On the senate of a good prince.

reading: Handless statues sit here before the altars of the gods:
of these, the first has had her sight taken away.
Such were the signs of supreme Power and of the Sacred Senate,
devised by the men of Thebes.
Why do they sit? Because it befits judges to be grave,
calm in mind, and not to waver with a fickle spirit.
Why are they without hands? So that they may take no gifts, nor allow themselves
to be swayed by promises or bribes.
But the president is blind. Because, with ears alone, without
passion, he steadily carries out the Senate's commands.

145.motto: What Christ does not take, the treasury seizes.

reading: The tight hand of a greedy prince squeezes the moist
sponges, which it had itself soaked before.
It raises thieves to the very top: then restrains them,
so as to turn into his own treasury what was wrongly gained.

146.motto: The tyrant's wealth is the poverty of his subjects.

reading: What the spleen is to the human body, that, in the commonwealth,
Caesar had declared his treasury to be.
When the spleen grows, the rest of the body's limbs waste away.
When the treasury grows, the poverty of the citizens is revealed.
Chiron is said to have trained the sons of heroes, and great Achilles,
in his own stables.
A half-beast teacher, a half-man centaur —
such is fitting for whoever sits beside kings.
He is a beast, when he harms his allies, when he tramples enemies:
and he is a man, when he pretends before the people to be devoted.
That the king of wasps never fixes any sting,
and that he is twice the size in body of the others,
proves a clement rule, moderate kingdoms,
and sacred laws entrusted to good judges.
The Epidaurian, son of Phoebus, sits on the raised altars,
mild, and the god is concealed in a huge serpent.
The sick run to him, and pray that the health-bringer may come:
he nods assent, and makes their prayers come true.
At Caesar's death, as though liberty had been regained,
this coin was struck under the leadership of the Bruti.
Foremost are little daggers, above which stands a cap,
such as slaves receive when freed by the hand [of their master].
Weep now more than usual over the misfortunes of human life,
Heraclitus: it teems with more evils.
You, on the other hand (now, if ever), raise your laughter,
Democritus: it has become even more ridiculous.
Meanwhile, seeing all this, I ponder with what end at last
I should weep with you, or how I should laugh with you from the heart.

152.motto: Sometimes life must be ransomed with money.

reading: Slow on his feet, with a swollen, hanging belly,
the beaver nevertheless escapes ambushes by this art.
He himself bites off with his teeth his own medicinal testicles,
and casts them away, knowing he is hunted for their sake.
From his example you will learn not to spare your possessions,
and, to ransom your life, to give money to your enemies.

153.motto: One should not wrestle with ghosts.

reading: Hector, dying from the blow of Aeacides' [Achilles'] spear-point —
he who had so often before conquered his enemies —
could not hold back his voice, as they taunted him,
preparing to bind cords to the chariot and to his feet.
"Tear me apart as you please: thus even timid hares
pluck the beard of a lion bereft of light [life]."
Death was wandering, joined with her companion Cupid. With her
Death carried quivers, and little Love carried the arrows.
They put up together for the night, and together they slept that one night,
blind was Love, and Death at that time was blind too.
For each, carelessly, took up the other's shafts:
Death holds the golden ones, the boy the bony weapons.
From this, an old man who should now belong to Acheron —
behold, he falls in love, and prepares flowery garlands for his head.
But I, because Love struck me with the exchanged bow,
am failing: the fates lay their hand on me too.
Spare me, boy; Death, holding your victorious standards, spare me.
Grant that I may love: grant that the old man descend to Acheron.

155.motto: On a beautiful woman snatched away by fate.

reading: Why, Death, did you dare to seize the boy Love by trickery?
So that he would hurl your weapons, thinking them his own.
The boy who, by his beauty, enticed and tormented tender girls,
more handsome, and noble throughout the whole city,
died before his time, to be mourned by no one more, Arestius,
than by you, to whom he was joined in chaste love.
Therefore you raise for him a tomb, a monument of so great a grief,
and strike the stars with plaintive cries.
"Do you leave without me, beloved? Shall we go together no more?
Will you no longer spend pleasant leisure with me in study?"
But the earth will cover you, and of your fate the Gorgon's face
and the dolphins will give mournful tokens.
A square stone, a most solid block, is set into the ground,
above which stands a curly-haired bust, down to the chest,
and it declares that it yields to no one: such
is Terminus, the single goal that drives men.
The day is unmoved, and the times are fixed beforehand by the fates,
and the last things pass judgment on the first.

158.motto: The inheritance of a rich man.

reading: On one side the Trojans drag off Patroclus in his borrowed armor,
on the other his comrades, and the whole Pelasgian [Greek] crowd, forbid it.
Hector gets the spoils, and the Greeks the corpse.
This same little drama is played out when a wealthy man dies.
The greatest quarrel arises, but at last the heir settles it,
and leaves something for the crows and the vultures too.
The elm, withered with age, and also bare of leaves,
has been embraced by the vine, shady with its green foliage.
It acknowledges the turns of nature: and, grateful to its
parent, returns the mutual rights of duty.
By this example it warns us to seek such friends
as not even our last day may part from the bond.
The blind man carries on his shoulders the lame man he has lifted up:
and repays this service for the use of his companion's eyes.
What either lacks, each supplies in harmony:
this one lends eyes, that one lends feet.
I diligently escaped two dangers with a single weapon,
when I was hard pressed on land, and when I was hard pressed on sea.
The shield kept me safe from the battle line; the same shield,
seized by me, carried me, shipwrecked, all the way to shore.
The three Graces attend upon Venus, and follow their mistress,
and from this prepare pleasures and sustenance for her.
Euphrosyne is joy, Aglaia is splendid radiance,
Pithus [Peitho] is persuasion, and charming grace of speech.
Why are they naked? Because beauty consists in the purity of the mind,
and pleases through its rare simplicity.
Or is it because the ungrateful return nothing: and an empty casket
belongs to the Graces? He who gives gifts is himself, naked, in need.
Why were winged sandals recently added to their feet? He who gives quickly
gives twice. A favour slow in coming is worth little.
Why does one, with arms entwined, face the other way? The grateful man
lends at interest: for him, as one departs, two remain.
Jupiter is their father; from the seed of heaven, Eurynome
bore the goddesses, accepted by all.
Whip-wielding blockheads, and stupid masters,
dare to vomit the bile of their impure breast upon me.
What should I do? Return the same? But would they not say
that I caught a noisy cicada with a single wing?
What good is it to drive off flies with laborious fanning?
It is better to disregard what you cannot destroy.
At night the dog looks at the moon's disk, as at a mirror,
and, seeing itself, believes there is another dog up there,
and barks: but the useless voice is scattered in vain upon the winds,
and deaf Diana runs her course.
A torrent was sweeping away pots, one of which was made of metal,
and the other was earthen, made by a potter's hand.
So the one [of metal] asks the other [of clay]: that it be willing to be carried close to it,
so that, joined together, both might withstand the rushing waters.
To him the clay one [replies]: "I have no wish for dealings with you,
lest this closeness bring me much harm.
For whether the wave carries you to me, or me to you,
I alone, being fragile, shall be shattered, while you remain unharmed."

166.motto: On one who perished by the cruelty of his own kind.

reading: The tide drove me, a dolphin, unwilling, onto the shore,
an example of how great the dangers are on the treacherous sea.
For if Neptune himself spares not even his own nurslings,
who would think men safe aboard their ships?

167.motto: Ἐχθρῶν ἄδωρα δῶρα (“Enemies' gifts are no gifts”). On the gifts of enemies.

reading: They say that in turn shield-bearing Ajax and Hector of Troy
began an exchange of war's memorial gifts.
Priam's son [Hector] received the belt, the son of Telamon [Ajax] the stern sword:
each received the instrument of his own death.
For the sword finished off Ajax, while dead Hector
was dragged by the thongs bound to Thessalian wheels.
Thus the gifts that enemies, under the title of courtesy, send to enemies
carry within them foreknowledge of fates to come.

greek.original: Εχθρῶν ἄδωρα δῶρα, In dona hostium.
greek.translation: Enemies' gifts are no gifts. On the gifts of enemies.

168.motto: Even the smallest should be feared.

reading: The beetle wages war, and itself provokes the enemy,
and though inferior in strength, prevails by strategy.
For, unseen and unrecognized, it hides itself in the eagle's feathers,
so as to reach the enemy's nest amid the highest stars.
And, piercing the eggs, it stops the hope of offspring from growing,
and in this way, having avenged the disgrace inflicted on it, departs.
The gilthead seizes little sardines in the open sea,
unless, frightened, they flee and head for the surface of the sea.
But there they become food for voracious gulls and coots.
Alas, weakness remains unprotected on every side.
All else will fall silent, and the sheep's hide will be mute,
if drums made of wolf's skin sound forth.
The sheepskin dreads this one so much that its enemy,
though lifeless, it cannot bear, lifeless as it is itself.
Thus Cischas [Žižka], his skin stripped off and turned into drums,
was able to defeat the Bohemian prelates.
While the Cyclops sits in the winding depths of his cave,
he sings this to himself among the gentle sheep:
"Graze on your grass; I shall feed on my Greek companions,
and last of all they will bring Utis [“Nobody,” i.e. Ulysses] [?] into my belly."
The man of Ithaca [Ulysses] heard this, and left the Cyclops bereft
of sight. Behold how punishment finds its own author!
A crow was carrying off through the swift air, caught in its claw,
a scorpion, a prize won by its bold gullet.
But the scorpion, slowly pouring its poison through the bird's limbs,
as an avenger drove its captor into the waters of the Styx.
A thing worthy of laughter indeed: he who was preparing death for others
perished himself, and fell victim to his own tricks.

173.motto: The guilt of the instigator equals that of the wrongdoer.

reading: A victorious crowd holds captive in a foul prison
a herald, who blew war-signals on his horn.
To them he makes his excuse: that he is not himself skilled in arms,
nor has he wounded anyone's side with a cruel sword.
To this they reply: "On the contrary, you, most cowardly one, sin more,
you who with the blare of brass rouse others to arms."

174.motto: One man sins, another is punished.

reading: As a puppy snatches up a stone and worries it with its bite,
yet does no harm in return to the one who threw it.
So most people let their true enemies slip away,
and with their teeth attack those burdened by no guilt at all.
Ajax, sword in hand, stood in the midst of a bristly herd,
slaughtering swine, believing he was slaughtering the sons of Tantalus [the Atridae].
Thus the pig, as a substitute victim, paid the penalty
for the son of Laertes [Ulysses], and for [?] (pro cavea).
Madness does not know how to harm its enemies; it misses its mark,
and, bereft of reason, rushes to its own ruin.
The elephant, with tower-bearing shoulders, and with its tusk of ivory,
which is accustomed fiercely to prevail in the wars of Mars,
has now placed its neck under the yoke, and, subdued by the goad,
draws Caesar's chariot to the sacred temples.
Even the wild beast recognizes that nations are everywhere at peace,
and, having cast aside its weapons, performs the duties of peace.
Behold the helmet which a fearless soldier once wore, and which
was often spattered with the blood of enemies.
Now that peace has been won, it has been given over to the bees for the use
of a slender hive: and it holds honeycombs and pleasing honey.
Let weapons lie far away: then let it be lawful to take up war,
when otherwise you cannot enjoy the benefits of peace.
Weave slender garlands from large ears of grain,
around which let a vine's tendril wind in turn.
Adorned with these, the halcyons, upon the wave of a sea calm as marble,
build their nests, and tend their chicks and unfledged young.
The year will be joyful for Ceres, and fruitful too for Bacchus,
if the king is like the sea-bird.

179.motto: It is wicked for the learned to revile the learned.

reading: Why, alas, cruel Procne, do you seize the melodious cicada,
and prepare a dreadful dish for your young?
Shrill one, you harm the shrilling one, vernal one the vernal one, guest
the guest, feathered bird the winged bird?
So cast aside this prey. For it is the gravest
wickedness for musical hearts to perish by one another's bite.
His left hand holds a bow; his right hand bears a stiff club,
and the Nemean lion covers his bare body.
This, then, is the likeness of Hercules. But it does not fit
that he bears temples old and white with age.
What of this: that his tongue is pierced by light chains,
by which he draws compliant men by their pierced ears?
Is it because the Gauls relate that Alcides, by tongue, not strength,
excelling, gave laws to the peoples?
Weapons yield to the toga, and even the hardest hearts
he, powerful in eloquence, draws them to his own wishes.
This antidote against the drugged cups of Aeaean Circe
was said, by report, to have been given by Mercury to the man of Ithaca.
They call it moly: it is pulled up with difficulty, its root black,
itself purple; but its flower has the look of milk.
The brightness of eloquence and fluent speech allures everyone:
but it is a matter of much toil, a work of such great labor.
Old man of Pallene, Proteus, whose shape is that of an actor,
who now bear the limbs of a man, now the limbs of a beast.
Tell me, come, what cause turns you into every form,
so that, ever-changing, you have no fixed shape at all?
I bear the marks of antiquity, of the earliest age:
about which each man dreams according to his own fancy.
There are those who bear on their family shields the bird of Jupiter,
there are those for whom the Serpent or the Lion furnishes the device.
But let these fierce creatures keep away from the seals of Poets,
and let the beautiful Swan uphold their learned coats-of-arms instead.
This one is sacred to Phoebus, and a nursling of our own region:
once a king, it still keeps its ancient titles.
A man of Locri dedicated to you, Delphic Phoebus, a cicada —
Eunomus did this, a fitting token of his victorious palm.
He competed with the plectrum, matched against his rival Sparthis,
and the strings, struck by his thumb, gave forth their sound.
When the worn string began to screech with a hoarse buzzing
and to spoil the rightful harmony and melody,
then a sweet, chirping winged creature settled on the cithara —
a cicada, which filled the broken string with its voice.
Drawn by the sound, it had come down from the high
woods, so that its chirping might bring us help.
So that the honor of your cicada, O holy one, might stand firm,
here, upon the cithara, the bronze musician herself sits.

185.motto: The letter kills, the spirit gives life.

reading: When Cadmus entrusted the viper's teeth to the fields
and sowed the dire seeds in the Aonian soil,
an armored host of earth-born men sprang up,
who fell by each other's hostile hand.
Those who, warned by Tritonis, threw down their arms
escaped, and were granted peace, and joined their right hands.
The son of Agenor was first to hand down to teachers the letters and signs,
and joined to them a pleasing harmony.
Their pupils, though, are troubled by very many contrary things,
which are resolved only by the help of Pallas.

186.motto: The sayings of the Seven Sages.

reading: Keep this in mind, you who would depict the sayings of the Seven Sages
and celebrate them in pictures.
'In all things measure is best' (as Cleobulus says) —
this the tongue of the balance, or the level, teaches.
'Know thyself' — so the Spartan Chilon bade each man.
Mirrors held in the hand, and glasses taken up, will convey this.
What Periander the Corinthian says — 'put a rein on anger' —
pennyroyal, held to the nostrils, will accomplish.
But Pittacus said: 'nothing too much.' The same thing is told
by those who melt grains of nigella with pursed mouth.
Solon bids us look back to the end. The last boundary-stone
in the fields, Terminus, would not yield even to mighty Jove himself.
Alas, how true Bias's word is: 'great is the multitude of the wicked' —
make a Sardinian horseman sit upon a mouflon.
'Be no man's surety' (Thales said): thus, smeared with birdlime,
the owl and the bee-eater draw their companion into the snares.
What monster is this? It is the Sphinx. Why does it have the bright face of a maiden,
the wings of birds, and the legs of a lion?
Ignorance of things has put on this shape: for so great
an evil has, of course, a threefold cause and origin.
Some are made ignorant by a shallow mind, some by beguiling pleasure,
and some by a proud heart.
But those to whom it is known what the Delphic inscription can mean
cut the dread throat of the headlong monster.
For man himself is at once two-footed, three-footed, and four-footed,
and the wise man's first laurel is to know man.
A fox, having slipped into the workshop of a mask-maker,
found a human head, skilfully polished,
so elegantly crafted that it lacked only
breath — in all else it would have seemed alive.
When she had taken it up in her paws, she said:
'What a head this is — but it has no brain.'
Phrixus, seated on the precious fleece, swims across the waters,
and fearlessly rides the golden ram across the sea.
What does this mean? A man dull of understanding, but rich in treasure,
governed by the judgment of a wife or a servant.
Behold the girl, joined to her husband by the right hand. Behold
how she sits: how a little dog plays at her feet?
This is the image of fidelity: and if Venus's ardor nurtures it,
then a branch of apples in her left hand will not be out of place.
For apples indeed belong to Venus; with them Hippomenes won
Schoeneis. So too Galathea aimed at her man [with an apple].
When it burns with passion, the viper takes its place on the seashore
and vomits forth its dread venom from its belly.
Summoning the moray, it raises a loud hissing,
but she at once seeks her mate's embrace.
The greatest reverence is owed to the marriage bed; spouses
owe each other mutual compliance as well.
A plaything for boys throwing stones — thus did
rustic care set me, a walnut tree, at the crossroads.
Tall, with torn branches and stripped bark, I
am pelted from every side, in rivalry, with slings.
What could happen more shameful to a barren tree? Alas,
unhappy me: I bear fruit to my own harm.
Before the spring day, in the north wind's
cold, the grey wood-pigeon builds her nest and warms her too-early eggs:
and so her chicks may lie the softer, she plucks her own feathers,
by which she herself, left bare, grows weak from the winter frost.
Are you not ashamed, Colchian woman, or you, wicked Procne? For death
a mere bird undergoes, out of love for her own offspring.

194.motto: The devotion of children toward their parents.

reading: Through the midst of his country's enemies, as he carried from the fire,
the sweet burden of his father on his shoulders, Aeneas
kept saying: 'Spare us: from seizing an old man you
will win no glory at all; but I, by rescuing my father, win the highest.'

195.motto: A woman's fame, not her beauty, should be made known.

reading: Kindly Venus, what is this image, what does that
tortoise signify, which you, goddess, press with your soft foot?
Phidias fashioned me thus, and ordered that the female
sex be known by my image.
And because it befits young women to stay at home, and to be silent,
he set such a sign beneath my feet.
Penelope, betrothed, wished to follow Ulysses,
had not her father Icarius preferred to keep her with him.
He offers Ithaca, this one offers Sparta. The maiden remains in anguish:
on one side her father, on the other her husband's mutual love press upon her.
So, sitting, she veils her face, hides her eyes.
These were the signs of modest shame.
By which Icarius knew that Ulysses had been preferred to himself,
and in this very pose he set up an altar to Modesty.
'May the gods grant better things to the pious!' Mezentius, why do you
force me so? Because a son-in-law was bought for you with a dowry —
one whom dreadful Gallic scabs [the 'French disease'] and the chin-disease consume:
what else is this (tell me, cruel father),
than to join dead bodies to living ones,
and to renew the savage deeds of the Etruscan chieftain?
The shape of the turning-post, and the very name Cypress,
show that one's own people are to be treated on equal terms [a play on words: the Greek name of the cypress, kyparissos, was linked with parisos, 'equal'].
Another.
The Cypress is a mournful tree, gracing the monuments of the great,
just as parsley is wont to adorn with its leaves the graves of the common people.
Another.
Its foliage is beautiful, and its leaves arranged in beautiful order,
but this beautiful foliage bears no fruit at all.
The oak is dear to Jupiter, who both preserves and cherishes us;
to one who has saved a citizen, a crown of oak leaves is given.
Another.
With its acorns it once fed the men of old; now it serves only for shade —
so, even so, Jupiter's tree is of service.
Because Homer used to call the willow the 'fruit-destroyer,'
it resembles men of Clitorian ways.
